t.6.59.1: Seeing his own army shaken and in tumult, a sight that made the hair stand on end, and seeing his brothers, whose valour equalled Śakra's, slain,
t.6.59.2: And having also seen his two paternal uncles, the brothers Mahodara and Mahāpārśva, bulls among rākṣasas, struck down in battle,
t.6.59.3: And Atikāya, of great splendour, resembling a mountain, who had received a boon from Brahmā and who crushed the pride of the gods and Dānavas, grew enraged in battle.
t.6.59.4: Mounting a chariot that blazed like a mass of a thousand suns, he, the foe of Śakra, rushed upon the monkeys.
t.6.59.5: Crowned and wearing polished earrings, he stretched his mighty bow, proclaimed his name aloud, and roared with a tremendous sound.
t.6.59.7: Beholding his form, like that of Viṣṇu at the time of his three strides, all those monkeys, stricken with fear, flee in the ten directions.
t.6.59.6: With that lion-like roar, with the proclaiming of his name, and with the terrible twang of his bowstring, he struck terror into the monkeys.
t.6.59.8: Encountering Atikāya, the monkeys, their minds bewildered, went for refuge in battle to the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, the giver of refuge.
t.6.59.9: Then Kākutstha saw from afar Atikāya, the bowman, mountain-like, standing in his chariot and roaring like a dark storm-cloud.
t.6.59.10: Rāghava, greatly astonished at seeing that great-souled one, first reassured the vānaras and then spoke to Vibhīṣaṇa.
t.6.59.11: Who is that one, resembling a mountain, bearing a bow, with tawny eyes, standing on a vast chariot yoked with a thousand horses?
t.6.59.12: That one who shines, surrounded by sharpened spears and by very keen, blazing darts and lances, like Maheśvara surrounded by his host of bhūtas.
t.6.59.13: He who shines forth here, surrounded by chariot-spears that gleam like the tongue of Kāla, is like a rain-cloud ringed with flashes of lightning.
t.6.59.14: His strung bows, gold-backed, on every side adorn his excellent chariot, as Śakra's bow spanning it adorns the sky.
t.6.59.15: Who is this tiger among rākṣasas, foremost of chariot-warriors, who approaches, illuminating the battlefield, on a chariot with the splendor of the sun?
t.6.59.17: And his bow shines forth, bent in three places, thundering like a cloud, its back of gold, richly adorned, resembling the bow of Śatakratu.
t.6.59.16: He shines forth with Rāhu set upon the peak of his banner, making the ten directions blaze with arrows that gleam like the rays of the sun.
t.6.59.18: That great chariot, with its flagstaff and its banners and its undercarriage, yoked with four horses, gave forth a roar like the thundering of clouds.
t.6.59.19: Twenty and ten and eight quivers were placed upon the chariot, along with fearsome bows and bowstrings tawny as gold.
t.6.59.20: Two swords also lay in the chariot, set at its sides and adorning its flanks, fitted with hilts four hands long and measuring a full ten hands in length.
t.6.59.22: With his two arms bound with golden armlets, this one shines like Himavān, the best of mountains, with its two lofty peaks.
t.6.59.21: Wearing a red cord about his neck, steadfast and like a great mountain, dark, with a huge mouth like that of Death, he looks like the sun stationed within a cloud.
t.6.59.23: And he whose face, with its lovely eyes, shines between its two earrings like the full disc of the moon passing between the two stars of Punarvasu.
t.6.59.24: Tell me, O mighty-armed one, about this foremost of rākṣasas, at the sight of whom all the vānaras, stricken with fear, have fled in every direction.
t.6.59.25: Thus questioned by the prince Rāma of immeasurable splendor, the greatly splendid Vibhīṣaṇa explained to Rāghava.
t.6.59.26: Ten-necked Rāvaṇa, the king of exceeding splendour, the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, terrible in deeds and of mighty energy.
t.6.59.27: He had a valiant son, equal to Rāvaṇa in battle, who served his elders, retained what he had learned, and was the foremost among those skilled in all weapons.
t.6.59.28: He is esteemed on horseback, in the chariot and on the elephant, with the sword, with the bow and in drawing it, and likewise in sowing dissension, in conciliation, in bestowing gifts, in statecraft and in counsel.
t.6.59.30: By him, his soul purified through austerity, Brahmā was propitiated; by him too were weapons obtained and enemies vanquished.
t.6.59.29: He on whose arm Laṅkā relies and so stands free of fear, this one they know as Atikāya, the son of Dhānyamālinī.
t.6.59.31: Svayambhū granted him invulnerability to gods and asuras; and this divine armour too, and this chariot, radiant as the sun.
t.6.59.32: By him the Devas and Dānavas have been defeated by the hundreds, the Rākṣasas have been protected, and the Yakṣas too have been slain.
t.6.59.33: He by whom, with his arrows, the thunderbolt of the wise Indra was checked, and likewise the noose of the lord of the waters was repelled in battle.
t.6.59.34: This is Atikāya, the mighty one, a bull among the Rākṣasas, the wise son of Rāvaṇa, who crushes the pride of the Devas and Dānavas.
t.6.59.35: Therefore, O bull among men, let an effort be made against him quickly, before he brings the monkey armies to destruction with his arrows.
t.6.59.36: Then the mighty Atikāya, having entered the army of the monkeys, twanged his bow and roared again and again.
t.6.59.37: Seeing him of terrible form, the best of chariot-warriors, standing in his chariot, the great-souled monkeys who were the foremost among them rushed upon him.
t.6.59.38: Kumuda, Dvivida, Mainda, Nīla, and Śarabha too, all at once rushed forward together with trees and mountain peaks.
t.6.59.39: Atikāya of great splendour, foremost among those skilled in weapons, cut down their trees and rocks with his arrows adorned with gold.
t.6.59.40: And that mighty night-roamer of terrible body, facing them in battle, pierced all those monkeys with arrows made entirely of iron.
t.6.59.41: Tormented by the shower of arrows, their bodies pierced, those monkeys were unable to retaliate against Atikāya in the great battle.
t.6.59.42: The rākṣasa terrified that army of monkey heroes, as an enraged lion in the fullness of his youth terrifies a herd of deer.
t.6.59.43: That lord of the rākṣasas, in the midst of the monkey army, struck down no one who was not fighting; approaching Rāma, bearing his bow and quiver, he spoke these proud words.
t.6.59.44: Standing in my chariot with arrows and bow in hand, I do not fight any ordinary warrior. Whoever has strength joined with resolve, let him give me battle swiftly, here and now.
t.6.59.45: Hearing those words of him as he spoke, Saumitri, the slayer of foes, grew angry; unable to endure it, he sprang up, and then, smiling, he seized his bow.
t.6.59.46: Enraged, Saumitri sprang up, drew an arrow from his quiver, and in front of Atikāya bent his mighty bow.
t.6.59.47: That fierce twang of Lakṣmaṇa's bowstring, filling the earth, the mountains, the sky, the ocean and the directions, struck terror into the night-wanderers.
t.6.59.48: Then, hearing the terrifying twang of Saumitri's bow, the mighty and greatly radiant son of the lord of the Rākṣasas was astonished.
t.6.59.49: Then Atikāya, enraged, seeing Lakṣmaṇa risen up, took a sharpened arrow and spoke these words.
t.6.59.50: You are a mere boy, O Saumitri, unskilled in feats of valour. Go away! Why do you wish to fight me, who am like Kāla himself?
t.6.59.51: Indeed, not even Himavān, nor the sky, nor the earth, is able to withstand the force of the missiles released by my arms.
t.6.59.53: Or if you, standing firm, do not wish to turn back, then stand, and casting off your life-breaths you shall go to the abode of Yama.
t.6.59.52: You wish to rouse the fire of universal destruction that sleeps peacefully. Lay down your bow and turn back; having come against me, do not throw away your life.
t.6.59.54: Behold my sharpened arrows, destroyers of the pride of foes, resembling the weapons of Īśvara and adorned with refined gold.
t.6.59.55: This serpent-like arrow will drink your blood, just as an enraged lord of beasts drinks the blood of the lord of elephants.
t.6.59.56: Having heard in battle the angry and arrogant words of Atikāya, the prince, exceedingly mighty and of great splendor, became enraged, and then he spoke words of great import.
t.6.59.57: Not by mere words do you become foremost, nor do men become noble through boasting. While I stand here, bow in hand and arrow in my grasp, show me your own strength, O wicked one!
t.6.59.58: Show yourself by your deeds; you ought not to boast. He who is endowed with true manliness is the one who is known as a hero.
t.6.59.59: Equipped with every kind of weapon, you stand mounted on your chariot, bow in hand. Whether with arrows or with divine missiles, display your valour!
t.6.59.60: Then with my sharpened arrows I shall strike down your head, just as the wind brings down from its stalk a palmyra fruit ripened by time.
t.6.59.62: Having concluded, "This is a mere boy," you ought not to disdain me. Whether I am a boy or an old man, know me to be death in battle.
t.6.59.61: Today my arrows, adorned with refined gold, will drink the blood from your body, the blood that wells up from within the wounds made by their arrowheads.
t.6.59.63: Hearing Lakṣmaṇa's words, well-reasoned and full of supreme meaning, Atikāya flew into a rage and took up an excellent arrow.
t.6.59.64: Then the Vidyādharas, the Bhūtas, the Devas, the Daityas, the great Ṛṣis and the high-souled Guhyakas beheld that battle.
t.6.59.65: Then Atikāya, enraged, fitted an arrow to his bow and loosed it at Lakṣmaṇa, as though contracting the very sky.
t.6.59.66: As that sharpened arrow, like a venomous serpent, came flying at him, Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, cut it down with a crescent-headed arrow.
t.6.59.67: Seeing that arrow cut down, like a serpent whose coils had been severed, Atikāya, greatly enraged, took up five arrows.
t.6.59.68: The night-ranger hurled those arrows at Lakṣmaṇa, but the younger brother of Bharata cut them down with sharp arrows before they could reach him.
t.6.59.69: Having cut those down with sharp arrows, Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, took up a whetted arrow that seemed to blaze with splendor.
t.6.59.70: Taking it up, Lakṣmaṇa fitted it to his excellent bow, drew it back with force, and released the arrow.
t.6.59.71: With an arrow of smooth joints, released from a bow drawn to its full length, that mighty one struck the foremost of the Rākṣasas on the forehead.
t.6.59.72: That arrow, sunk into the forehead of that fearsome Rākṣasa and smeared with blood, appeared in the battle like a lord of serpents.
t.6.59.73: And the rākṣasa, shaken by Lakṣmaṇa's arrows, trembled like the dreadful gate-tower of Tripura struck by Rudra's arrow.
t.6.59.74: Recovering his breath, the mighty one reflected and considered, and said: “Well done! By the striking of your arrows you have proven an enemy worthy of my praise.”
t.6.59.75: Having reflected thus, he bent his face and bent both his arms, and, mounting the seat of his chariot, he drove about in his chariot.
t.6.59.76: One, three, five, seven arrows at a time the bull among rākṣasas took up, fitted to his bow, drew back and released.
t.6.59.77: Those arrows, resembling Death itself, loosed from the bow of the lord of the rākṣasas, golden-feathered and blazing like the sun, made the sky seem as if aflame.
t.6.59.78: Then Rāvaṇa's younger brother, unperturbed, cut down those floods of arrows released by the rākṣasa with many sharpened arrows of his own.
t.6.59.79: Seeing those arrows cut down in battle, the son of Rāvaṇa, foe of the lord of the thirty gods, grew enraged and seized a sharpened arrow.
t.6.59.80: Having fitted that arrow to his bow, the greatly splendid one swiftly released it, and then struck Saumitri, who was advancing, in the middle of the chest.
t.6.59.81: Struck on the chest in battle by Atikāya, Saumitri streamed forth blood copiously, like an elephant in rut streaming forth its ichor.
t.6.59.82: Then the mighty one swiftly freed himself of the arrows lodged in his body; he took up a sharp arrow and charged it with a divine missile.
t.6.59.83: Then he charged his arrow with the fiery missile of Agni; at once that arrow blazed forth, and so did the bow of that great-souled one.
t.6.59.84: Atikāya, exceedingly splendid, took up the solar weapon, and with it he charged an arrow that resembled a serpent and bore golden feathers.
t.6.59.85: Then Lakṣmaṇa hurled that blazing, terrible arrow, which he had set to his bow, at Atikāya, as Antaka, the Ender, hurls the rod of Time.
t.6.59.86: Seeing the arrow charged with the fire-weapon, the night-wanderer then released a blazing arrow joined with the Sūrya-weapon.
t.6.59.88: Having consumed each other in flames, those two excellent arrows fell upon the surface of the earth; reduced to ashes and bereft of their blaze, they no longer shone.
t.6.59.87: In the sky those two clashed, arrow against arrow, striking one another, their tips blazing with fiery energy like two enraged serpents.
t.6.59.89: Then Atikāya, enraged, released the Aiṣīka weapon; the valiant Saumitri cut that weapon down with the Aindra weapon.
t.6.59.90: Seeing his Aiṣīka weapon struck down, the prince, the son of Rāvaṇa, grew furious and fitted an arrow charged with the missile of Yama.
t.6.59.91: Then the night-wanderer hurled that missile at Lakṣmaṇa, but Lakṣmaṇa struck down that missile with the missile of Vāyu.
t.6.59.92: Then the enraged Lakṣmaṇa rained down upon him, the son of Rāvaṇa, torrents of arrows, as a cloud pours down torrents of rain.
t.6.59.93: Those arrows, reaching Atikāya and striking his armor adorned with diamonds, suddenly fell to the surface of the earth, their pointed heads shattered.
t.6.59.94: Seeing those arrows rendered futile, the greatly renowned Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes, rained down a thousand arrows.
t.6.59.95: Though showered with floods of arrows, the mighty rākṣasa Atikāya, whose armor could not be pierced, was not in the least shaken in battle.
t.6.59.96: The best of men could not inflict any pain on him in battle. Then Vāyu approached him and spoke these words.
t.6.59.97: For this one has been granted a boon by Brahmā and is clad in armor that cannot be destroyed. Pierce him with the Brahmā weapon, for he cannot be slain any other way.
t.6.59.98: Then, having heard the words of Vāyu, Saumitri, whose valor was equal to Indra's, took up an arrow of unfailing force, swiftly yoking to it that Brāhma weapon.
t.6.59.99: As Saumitri fitted that supreme missile to his excellent sharp-pointed arrow, the quarters, together with the moon, the sun and the great planets, and the sky trembled, and the earth cried out.
t.6.59.100: Having charged that well-feathered arrow, like a messenger of Yama, with the weapon of Brahmā and fixed it on his bow, Saumitri loosed the shaft, like a thunderbolt, in battle at that son of Indra's foe.
t.6.59.101: Then in the battle Atikāya saw that arrow loosed by Lakṣmaṇa rushing toward him, of unfailing speed and blazing like fire, its feathered shaft splendidly adorned with gold and the finest diamonds.
t.6.59.102: Watching him, Atikāya suddenly struck him with many sharpened arrows. Then that arrow of his, swift as Suparṇa, flew with tremendous speed to his side.
t.6.59.103: Then Atikāya, seeing that arrow approaching, blazing and like Antaka, Death himself, at the time of destruction, struck at it with spears, swords, maces and axes, with tridents and with ploughshares too, his vigour undiminished.
t.6.59.104: That arrow, blazing like fire, rendered vain those weapons of wondrous form, and then, overpowering him, carried off the very head of Atikāya, adorned with its diadem.
t.6.59.105: That head, helmet and all, struck down by Lakṣmaṇa's arrow, suddenly fell to the ground like a peak of Himavat.
t.6.59.106: Then many monkeys, filled with great joy, their faces like full-blown lotuses, honored Lakṣmaṇa, who had attained his desired goal, now that the enemy of terrible strength, so hard to approach, had been slain.
